Note: Dal latino TOLLERE, come l’italiano togliere e l’antico tòrre; nel nord ha preso il senso di «prendere» e poi «comprare» (cfr. l’antico tòrre moglie, e nel corso «Chi tö miée da bunura», 15a leziun). Si coniuga come fà, dà, na: radice con -g- (töghem, töghendu, tögaria) e participio in -i (töi, come fai, dai, nai).
Note_English: From Latin TOLLERE, like Italian togliere and the older tòrre; in the north it came to mean ‘take’ and then ‘buy’ (compare old Italian tòrre moglie, ‘take a wife’, and in the course «Chi tö miée da bunura», lesson 15). It conjugates like fà, dà, na: a stem with -g- (töghem, töghendu, tögaria) and a participle in -i (töi, like fai, dai, nai).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Riflessivo di töö con fö («togliersi di torno»); si coniuga come töö.
Note_English: The reflexive of töö with fö (‘get out of the way’); it conjugates like töö.
Source: Claude; the imperative forms are the course's (imperativo l.152)

Note: Dal latino BIBERE, come l’italiano bere (antico bevere); la -v- torna in bevi, bevum. La -f finale è la -v diventata sorda in fine di parola, come in möf, scrif, vif.
Note_English: From Latin BIBERE, like Italian bere (older bevere); the -v- comes back in bevi, bevum. The final -f is -v made voiceless at the end of a word, as in möf, scrif, vif.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Come l’italiano bramare, di origine germanica.
Note_English: Like Italian bramare, of Germanic origin.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Da camin «cammino», dal tardo latino CAMMINUS, parola di origine celtica.
Note_English: From camin ‘way’, Late Latin CAMMINUS, a word of Celtic origin.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino CANTARE; come quasi tutti i verbi in -à continua la prima coniugazione latina in -ARE.
Note_English: From Latin CANTARE; like nearly all verbs in -à it continues the Latin first conjugation in -ARE.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino CAPERE «prendere, contenere», passato alla coniugazione in -ire; come l’italiano capisco prende -is- (capisi, ta capissat).
Note_English: From Latin CAPERE ‘take, hold’, moved into the -ire conjugation; like Italian capisco it takes -is- (capisi, ta capissat).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: catà viene dal latino CAPTARE «cercare di prendere» (da cui anche il francese acheter, comprare); con fö «fuori» vuol dire scegliere, letteralmente «prendere fuori».
Note_English: catà comes from Latin CAPTARE ‘try to catch’ (also the source of French acheter, buy); with fö ‘out’ it means choose, literally ‘take out’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal tardo latino CIRCARE «andare intorno», da CIRCA.
Note_English: From Late Latin CIRCARE ‘go around’, from CIRCA.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Come l’italiano acchiappare, di origine discussa. È il verbo comune per «prendere»; töö vuol dire soprattutto «comprare».
Note_English: Like Italian acchiappare, of disputed origin. It is the everyday verb for ‘take’; töö mostly means ‘buy’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino CURRERE, con la caduta della vocale finale, come cred, met, vif.
Note_English: From Latin CURRERE, with the final vowel lost, as in cred, met, vif.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino CREDERE.
Note_English: From Latin CREDERE.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino *COMINITIARE (CUM + INITIARE «iniziare»), come l’italiano cominciare. Si dice anche tacà, «attaccare» (cfr. l’italiano attaccare a parlare).
Note_English: From Latin *COMINITIARE (CUM + INITIARE ‘begin’), like Italian cominciare. Also tacà, ‘attach’ (compare Italian attaccare a parlare, ‘start talking’).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino CONSUERE (nel latino parlato *COSIRE), come l’italiano cucire. Come capì prende -is- (cüsisi).
Note_English: From Latin CONSUERE (spoken Latin *COSIRE), like Italian cucire. Like capì it takes -is- (cüsisi).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Da cüsina, dal tardo latino COCINA (COQUINA) «cucina». Nelle lezioni si dice anche fà da mangià.
Note_English: From cüsina, Late Latin COCINA (COQUINA) ‘kitchen’. The lessons also say fà da mangià.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Come l’italiano adoperare, da OPERA «lavoro». La radice è lunga dove cade l’accento (al dupera) e breve altrove (duprà, dupraa).
Note_English: Like Italian adoperare, from OPERA ‘work’. The stem is long where the stress falls (al dupera) and short elsewhere (duprà, dupraa).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino DEBERE, che ha perso la -b-; una -v- ritorna in ta devat, duvüü.
Note_English: From Latin DEBERE, which has lost its -b-; a -v- comes back in ta devat, duvüü.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino DARE. Come fà, stà e na ha forme brevi (dò, ta de, la da) e il participio in -i (dai).
Note_English: From Latin DARE. Like fà, stà and na it has short forms (dò, ta de, la da) and a participle in -i (dai).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino DICERE: la -s- di disi, al diseva continua la -C- latina (come in italiano dicevo).
Note_English: From Latin DICERE: the -s- of disi, al diseva continues the Latin -C- (as in Italian dicevo).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino DORMIRE. A differenza di capì non prende -is- (dormi, ta dormat).
Note_English: From Latin DORMIRE. Unlike capì it does not take -is- (dormi, ta dormat).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino FACERE, ridotto come l’italiano fare, fo. Come dà, stà e na ha forme brevi (fò, ta fé) e il participio in -i (fai).
Note_English: From Latin FACERE, shortened like Italian fare, fo. Like dà, stà and na it has short forms (fò, ta fé) and a participle in -i (fai).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: fà + sü «su» (latino SURSUM): costruire, letteralmente «fare su». Si coniuga come fà.
Note_English: fà + sü ‘up’ (Latin SURSUM): build, literally ‘make up’. It conjugates like fà.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino JOCARI; la ö viene dalla O breve latina accentata, come in möf, föra, töö.
Note_English: From Latin JOCARI; the ö comes from a stressed Latin short O, as in möf, föra, töö.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Di origine germanica (*wardōn «stare in guardia»), come l’italiano guardare, il francese garder e l’inglese ward.
Note_English: Of Germanic origin (*wardōn ‘keep watch’), like Italian guardare, French garder and English ward.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino LAVARE.
Note_English: From Latin LAVARE.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Riflessivo di lavà: il pronome sa si unisce all’infinito (lavà + sa), come in italiano lavarsi.
Note_English: The reflexive of lavà: the pronoun sa is joined to the infinitive (lavà + sa), as in Italian lavarsi.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino LEGERE. La -n- (lenc, lengiüü) è della parlata; le lezioni scrivono le(n)gi, cioè con o senza n.
Note_English: From Latin LEGERE. The -n- (lenc, lengiüü) is local; the lessons write le(n)gi, that is, with or without the n.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: mandà (latino MANDARE «affidare») + giò «giù»: mandare giù, inghiottire, come in italiano.
Note_English: mandà ‘send’ (Latin MANDARE ‘entrust’) + giò ‘down’: send down, swallow, as in Italian mandar giù.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal francese antico mangier, dal latino MANDUCARE «masticare»; anche l’italiano mangiare viene dal francese.
Note_English: From Old French mangier, from Latin MANDUCARE ‘chew’; Italian mangiare also comes from French.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Da mazza (latino *MATTEA): «uccidere a colpi di mazza», come l’italiano ammazzare. Nelle lezioni anche copà.
Note_English: From mazza ‘club’ (Latin *MATTEA): ‘kill with a club’, like Italian ammazzare. The lessons also have copà.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino MINARE «spingere avanti (il bestiame)»; come l’italiano menare vuol dire sia condurre sia picchiare (vedi picà).
Note_English: From Latin MINARE ‘drive (cattle)’; like Italian menare it means both lead and hit (see picà).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino MITTERE «mandare», che nel latino parlato prese il senso di «mettere».
Note_English: From Latin MITTERE ‘send’, which in spoken Latin came to mean ‘put’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: met + insema «insieme» (latino IN SIMUL): unire. Si coniuga come met.
Note_English: met + insema ‘together’ (Latin IN SIMUL): join. It conjugates like met.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: met + sü «su»: indossare, letteralmente «mettere su». Si coniuga come met.
Note_English: met + sü ‘on, up’: put on (clothes), literally ‘put up’. It conjugates like met.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino MOVERE: la O breve accentata diventa ö, la -v finale diventa -f (möf, ma mövi).
Note_English: From Latin MOVERE: the stressed short O becomes ö, the final -v becomes -f (möf, but mövi).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Riflessivo di möf (möv- + sa).
Note_English: The reflexive of möf (möv- + sa).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Come l’italiano andare / vado mescola due verbi: na (andare senza an-) e le forme del latino VADERE (vo, ta ve, la va).
Note_English: Like Italian andare / vado it mixes two verbs: na (andare without an-) and the forms of Latin VADERE (vo, ta ve, la va).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: na + föra «fuori» (latino FORAS): uscire. Si coniuga come na, con l’ausiliare ves.
Note_English: na + föra ‘out’ (Latin FORAS): go out. It conjugates like na, with the auxiliary ves.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: na + giò «giù» (latino DEORSUM): scendere. Si coniuga come na, con l’ausiliare ves.
Note_English: na + giò ‘down’ (Latin DEORSUM): go down. It conjugates like na, with the auxiliary ves.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: na + sü «su» (latino SURSUM): salire. Si coniuga come na, con l’ausiliare ves.
Note_English: na + sü ‘up’ (Latin SURSUM): go up. It conjugates like na, with the auxiliary ves.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: na + innanz «innanzi, avanti» (latino IN ANTE): procedere. Si coniuga come na.
Note_English: na + innanz ‘forward’ (Latin IN ANTE): go on. It conjugates like na.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino NATARE, diventato *NOTARE nel latino parlato (italiano nuotare); la -t- tra vocali è diventata -d-, come spesso al nord.
Note_English: From Latin NATARE, spoken Latin *NOTARE (Italian nuotare); the -t- between vowels became -d-, as often in the north.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino NOMINARE, da NOMEN «nome».
Note_English: From Latin NOMINARE, from NOMEN ‘name’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino PACARE «pacificare»: pagando si mette in pace il creditore.
Note_English: From Latin PACARE ‘pacify’: paying settles the creditor.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino PARTIRE «dividere», poi «separarsi, andare via».
Note_English: From Latin PARTIRE ‘divide’, then ‘part, leave’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino PENSARE «pesare», poi «soppesare con la mente».
Note_English: From Latin PENSARE ‘weigh’, then ‘weigh in the mind’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal tardo latino PISTARE «pestare nel mortaio».
Note_English: From Late Latin PISTARE ‘pound in a mortar’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Voce imitativa del colpo, come l’italiano picchiare. Nelle lezioni anche menà.
Note_English: Imitates the sound of a blow, like Italian picchiare. The lessons also have menà.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino parlato *POTERE (latino classico POSSE); la -t- tra vocali è diventata -d-, come in nodà.
Note_English: From spoken Latin *POTERE (classical POSSE); the -t- between vowels became -d-, as in nodà.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino PRODUCERE; la U lunga latina diventa ü, come in tradü.
Note_English: From Latin PRODUCERE; the Latin long U becomes ü, as in tradü.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino RECORDARI (da COR «cuore»); la -c- tra vocali è diventata -g- (italiano ricordarsi).
Note_English: From Latin RECORDARI (from COR ‘heart’); the -c- between vowels became -g- (Italian ricordarsi).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino RESECARE «tagliare», da cui anche resega, la sega; la -c- tra vocali è diventata -g-.
Note_English: From Latin RESECARE ‘cut’, also the source of resega, a saw; the -c- between vowels became -g-.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino RESTARE «fermarsi».
Note_English: From Latin RESTARE ‘stay behind’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Di origine germanica (*raubōn), come l’italiano rubare e l’inglese rob.
Note_English: Of Germanic origin (*raubōn), like Italian rubare and English rob.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino SAPERE «avere sapore, essere saggio»; la -p- è diventata -v-. Le forme so, ta set, la sa sono brevi come l’italiano so, sa.
Note_English: From Latin SAPERE ‘taste, be wise’; the -p- became -v-. The forms so, ta set, la sa are short like Italian so, sa.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: s- + bat «battere» (latino BATTUERE). La grafia sc davanti a consonante (scbat, sctà) indica la s pronunciata come sc di scena, tipica del Ticino.
Note_English: s- + bat ‘beat’ (Latin BATTUERE). The spelling sc before a consonant (scbat, sctà) marks an s said like English sh, typical of Ticino.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Voce imitativa, come l’italiano schiacciare; dalla stessa radice il milanese schiscetta, il portavivande.
Note_English: Imitative, like Italian schiacciare; Milanese schiscetta, the lunch box, comes from the same root.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino AUSCULTARE, che ha perso la vocale iniziale (italiano ascoltare).
Note_English: From Latin AUSCULTARE, with the first vowel lost (Italian ascoltare).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino SCRIBERE; la -v- di scrivi diventa -f in fine di parola.
Note_English: From Latin SCRIBERE; the -v- of scrivi becomes -f at the end of a word.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino SCULPERE, passato alla coniugazione in -ire come l’italiano scolpire.
Note_English: From Latin SCULPERE, moved into the -ire conjugation like Italian scolpire.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal tardo latino SERARE, da SERA «chiavistello» (italiano serrare); in dialetto è il verbo comune per «chiudere».
Note_English: From Late Latin SERARE, from SERA ‘bolt’ (Italian serrare); in the dialect it is the everyday verb for ‘close’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Riflessivo con giò «giù»: letteralmente «mettersi a sedere giù». Probabilmente dalla radice del latino SEDERE; l’origine esatta non è certa.
Note_English: Reflexive with giò ‘down’: literally ‘sit oneself down’. Probably from the root of Latin SEDERE; the exact origin is uncertain.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino STARE. Come fà, dà e na ha forme brevi (sctò, ta sctét) e il participio in -i (sctai); sc indica la s pronunciata come in scena.
Note_English: From Latin STARE. Like fà, dà and na it has short forms (sctò, ta sctét) and a participle in -i (sctai); sc marks an s said like sh.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino SUDARE; la U lunga latina diventa ü (la süda).
Note_English: From Latin SUDARE; the Latin long U becomes ü (la süda).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: tacà «attaccare» + sü «su»: appendere. tacà vuol dire anche «cominciare» (vedi cumincià).
Note_English: tacà ‘attach’ + sü ‘up’: hang up. tacà also means ‘begin’ (see cumincià).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal tardo latino TALEARE (da TALEA «ramo tagliato»); il gli dell’italiano tagliare qui è i (tai, taium).
Note_English: From Late Latin TALEARE (from TALEA ‘cutting’); the gli of Italian tagliare is i here (tai, taium).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino TACERE; la -C- davanti a e è diventata -s-, come in dì (disi).
Note_English: From Latin TACERE; the -C- before e became -s-, as in dì (disi).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino TENERE, passato in -ì; gn come nell’italiano tengo e in vegnì.
Note_English: From Latin TENERE, moved into -ì; gn as in Italian tengo and in vegnì.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: tirà «tirare» + via: togliere, letteralmente «tirare via».
Note_English: tirà ‘pull’ + via ‘away’: take off, remove, literally ‘pull away’.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Riflessivo di tirà via (tirà + sa).
Note_English: The reflexive of tirà via (tirà + sa).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino TRADUCERE «portare oltre»; la U lunga latina diventa ü, come in prodü.
Note_English: From Latin TRADUCERE ‘carry across’; the Latin long U becomes ü, as in prodü.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino parlato *TROPARE «inventare» (cfr. trovatore), come l’italiano trovare; dove cade l’accento la o diventa ö (trövi).
Note_English: From spoken Latin *TROPARE ‘invent’ (compare troubadour), like Italian trovare; where the stress falls the o becomes ö (trövi).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: turnà «tornare» (latino TORNARE «girare al tornio») + indré «indietro» (latino IN DE RETRO).
Note_English: turnà ‘return’ (Latin TORNARE ‘turn on a lathe’) + indré ‘back’ (Latin IN DE RETRO).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino HONORARE; la o non accentata diventa spesso u (unurà, duprà / doprà).
Note_English: From Latin HONORARE; an unstressed o often becomes u (unurà, duprà / doprà).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino VIDERE; participio visct (italiano visto), con sc per la s come in sctà.
Note_English: From Latin VIDERE; participle visct (Italian visto), with sc for the s as in sctà.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino HABERE. La -gh è il ci dell’italiano ci ho: il dialetto dice sempre gò, ta ghé, la ga, e l’infinito vegh è (a)vé + ghe.
Note_English: From Latin HABERE. The -gh is the ci of Italian ci ho: the dialect always says gò, ta ghé, la ga, and the infinitive vegh is (a)vé + ghe.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino VENIRE; gn come nell’italiano vengo e in tegnì.
Note_English: From Latin VENIRE; gn as in Italian vengo and in tegnì.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Probabilmente dal latino APERIRE (participio APERTUM), con la caduta della a- iniziale. Da non confondere con vert «verde», dal latino VIRIDIS.
Note_English: Probably from Latin APERIRE (participle APERTUM), with the first a- lost. Not to be confused with vert ‘green’, from Latin VIRIDIS.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino ESSE (latino parlato *ESSERE); la v- iniziale si è aggiunta davanti alla vocale, come nel milanese vess.
Note_English: From Latin ESSE (spoken Latin *ESSERE); the initial v- was added before the vowel, as in Milanese vess.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino VIVERE; la -v finale diventa -f (la vif, ma vivum).
Note_English: From Latin VIVERE; the final -v becomes -f (la vif, but vivum).
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino parlato *VOLERE (latino classico VELLE); la O accentata diventa ö (vöri, la vö) e la -l- tra vocali è diventata -r-.
Note_English: From spoken Latin *VOLERE (classical VELLE); the stressed O becomes ö (vöri, la vö) and the -l- between vowels became -r-.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: vöré + sa + ben: volersi bene, amarsi. Si coniuga come vöré.
Note_English: vöré + sa + ben: love each other (Italian volersi bene). It conjugates like vöré.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Da vos «voce» (latino VOX), come l’italiano vociare.
Note_English: From vos ‘voice’ (Latin VOX), like Italian vociare.
Source: Claude, from general Romance etymology (not from the course); the forms are the course's

Note: Dal latino TRAHERE «tirare», come l’italiano trarre: in dialetto vuol dire gettare (trà via, buttare via; trà sü, vomitare). Si coniuga come fà: le forme di questa pagina sono ricavate da fà e dal milanese trà.
Note_English: From Latin TRAHERE ‘pull’, like Italian trarre: in the dialect it means throw (trà via, throw away; trà sü, throw up). It conjugates like fà: the forms on this page are worked out from fà and Milanese trà.
Source: Claude; Milanese forms from lmo.wiktionary.org (trà/coniugazzion)

Note: Riflessivo di guardà (guardà + sa), come l’italiano guardarsi: guardarsi allo specchio, o guardarsi l’un l’altro (Quand guardass in di öcc…, San Martin). Si coniuga come guardà e lavas.
Note_English: The reflexive of guardà (guardà + sa), like Italian guardarsi: look at oneself, or look at each other (Quand guardass in di öcc…, San Martin). It conjugates like guardà and lavas.
Source: Claude
